summary: Gives better guidance for choosing RTCP canonical names (CNAMEs), the persistent identifiers that tie an RTP endpoint's media streams together. The guidance in RFC 3550 was not enough to make names reliably unique within a session, so this document updates it, building on the earlier work in RFC 6222.

eli5.summary: Everyone in a video call needs a name tag that nobody else shares. This explains how to pick one that will not clash.

questions: how to choose an rtcp cname
what is an rtcp canonical name
how long should an rtcp cname be
subtitle: How RTP endpoints should pick RTCP CNAMEs that are unique, using random values instead of host names or addresses.

tldr.problem: RTCP CNAMEs are meant to be unique within an RTP session, but the RFC 3550 advice (fully qualified domain names, IPv4 addresses) often produces duplicates, and the RFC 6222 replacement was complicated and could be linked across sessions.
tldr.mechanism: An endpoint builds its CNAME from a UUID (long-term), or from a cryptographically pseudorandom value of at least 96 bits encoded in Base64 (short-term or per-session).
tldr.outcome: CNAMEs are unique with very high probability and simpler to generate. This document replaces RFC 6222 and updates RFC 3550.

today: RFC 7022 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6222 and updates RFC 3550. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why CNAME Advice Needed Fixing
sections.content:
The RTCP Canonical Name (CNAME) is a persistent transport-level identifier for an RTP endpoint. The SSRC of an endpoint may change if a collision is detected or when the application restarts, but the CNAME is meant to stay unchanged, so that endpoints can be identified and associated with their media streams.

For this to work, CNAMEs should be unique among the participants of an RTP session. RFC 3550 gave recommendations, but some of them do not guarantee uniqueness. RFC 6222 updated them, but later investigation showed that parts of its algorithm were unnecessarily complicated or ineffective, and could produce CNAMEs that are linkable across sessions. RFC 7022 replaces the algorithm in Section 5 of RFC 6222 with a simpler one.
sections.eli5: Everyone in a call needs a name tag no one else has. The old ways of picking one sometimes gave two people the same tag, so this RFC gives a better way.

sections.title: Problems With the Earlier Guidelines
sections.content:
RFC 3550 recommends a CNAME of the form user@host on multiuser systems, or host if the username is not available. The host part is the fully qualified domain name (FQDN). The RFC says FQDNs are no longer necessarily unique and can be shared by several endpoints in large service provider networks.

Using the numeric IPv4 address as the host part has a similar problem. Private address space (RFC 1918) means hosts may share addresses, and even public IPv4 addresses can be shared by several hosts behind a NAT device (RFC 3022). Hosts with private addresses behind an RTP-level translator could also end up with non-unique CNAMEs. RFC 3550 suggested a configuration option to let the user choose a unique name, but the text says experience shows this does not work well in practice.
sections.eli5: Using a computer's name or street address is like two kids in different houses both saying they live at 'the blue house'. The tag does not tell them apart.

sections.title: Persistent or Per-Session CNAMEs
sections.content:
A CNAME can either persist across RTP sessions for an endpoint, or be chosen fresh for each session.

An endpoint that sends several related streams that must be synchronized at the receiver MUST use the same CNAME for all of them. A common example is lip-sync: a participant uses one CNAME for both its audio session and its video session. Another is the layers of a layered audio codec. Unrelated streams in a session may use different CNAMEs.

A longer-term persistent CNAME helps third-party monitoring, such as network management tools correlating quality of service across sessions. An application that wants to discourage that can generate a new CNAME for each session or group of related sessions, which gives some limited privacy. The text notes that non-RTP means can still correlate sessions, so a determined traffic analyst is not stopped. Because CNAMEs are opaque strings to remote peers, there is no backward-compatibility issue with RFC 3550 implementations.
sections.eli5: If you send both a picture and a sound, you wear the same name tag on both so the other side can match them up. If you want to stay a bit more private, you wear a brand new tag every call.

sections.title: How to Build the CNAME
sections.content:
The IPv4 address as the host part is NOT RECOMMENDED. An endpoint that wants a persistent CNAME MUST use one of two methods:

  • Long-term: generate and store a UUID (RFC 4122) as the host part. It MUST be version 1, 2 or 4, with urn:uuid: stripped, giving a 36-octet printable string.
  • Short-term: generate an identifier with the procedure in Section 5, at least once per software initialization, then convert at least the least significant 96 bits to ASCII with Base64 (RFC 4648). With 96 bits the string is 16 octets, well under the 255-octet CNAME maximum.

For a per-session CNAME, the endpoint MUST generate a new one for every RTP session using the same procedure and Base64 conversion. It cannot change during the life of a session, and the user@ part is omitted. In the persistent cases, user@ MAY be omitted on single-user systems or replaced by an opaque token on multiuser systems for privacy.

The document does not let implementers invent their own method. A future specification might define another one, but it needs review and approval before deployment. These mechanisms are only for CNAMEs, not general-purpose unique identifiers.
sections.eli5: You can pick a very long serial number you keep forever, or a fresh random number each time you start up or join a call. Either way the number is long enough that nobody else will get the same one.

sections.title: Generating the Unique Identifier
sections.content:
The procedure is short: generate a cryptographically pseudorandom value as described in RFC 4086. The value MUST be at least 96 bits.

The hardest part is having a suitable cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG). Where one already exists, this is far simpler than the algorithm in RFC 6222. The RFC points out that SIP stacks must use cryptographically random numbers for To and From tags, that RTCWEB implementations need secure PRNGs for ICE and DTLS-SRTP, and that essentially every web browser already supports TLS, which requires one.
sections.eli5: Roll a huge number of dice with a really good dice machine and write down the result. That is your tag.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3550 apply. With random CNAMEs, participants will with very high probability have unique names, but nothing forces participants to choose well. Implementations therefore MUST NOT rely on CNAME uniqueness for any essential security service. A participant can pick a CNAME to impersonate another, and no recommendation can prevent that. SRTP (RFC 3711) keeps unauthorized entities out of a session but does not aim to stop impersonation by authorized ones.

A 96-bit value allows on the order of 2^{40} CNAMEs globally before there is a large chance of collision, with about a 50% chance of one collision after 2^{48} CNAMEs.

Earlier recommendations allowed a fixed CNAME, which let an attacker link separate sessions and undo the obfuscation of IPv6 privacy addresses or NAPT. This document no longer describes a way to make fixed values, so that linkage goes away, though it also makes it harder for traffic analysis devices that look for dropped or delayed packets to link sessions.
sections.eli5: A long random tag makes accidental mix-ups very unlikely. But someone could still copy another person's tag on purpose, so it should never be used as a password.
